formation.title: Aotearoa United
formation.text:
The iwi of Aotearoa have come together under a single sovereignty. For centuries, the tribes of these islands have lived as independent nations, trading pounamu and obsidian, waging war over mana and resources, building great pa on every strategic hilltop. Now, the shared identity of the Maori people has crystallized into something greater than any single iwi could achieve alone.

The question before us is what kind of nation Aotearoa will become. Shall we draw upon the warrior traditions that have defined our people: the haka, the taiaha, the unbreakable will of the toa? Or shall we look to the ocean that brought our ancestors here, building upon the navigational mastery and cultural traditions that make us unique among the peoples of the world?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: We are the children of Tu: strength through battle!

modifiers.name: Mana o te Toa
modifiers.text: The mana of warriors courses through the land. From the thundering haka to the flash of taiaha in battle, every iwi knows that strength and courage define who we are.

options.text: We are the children of Tangaroa: mastery of the sea!

modifiers.name: Mana o te Moana
modifiers.text: The ocean is our highway and our heritage. Our ancestors crossed the greatest sea on earth to reach these islands, and now the same navigational mastery guides our trade and exploration.

advances.name: Pa Engineering
advances.text: The science of building fortified hilltop settlements, pa, with multiple defensive terraces, palisades, and fighting stages.

advances.name: Toa Warriors
advances.text: The warrior tradition of the toa, elite fighters trained in mau rakau martial arts and wielding taiaha, mere, and tewhatewha.

advances.name: Waka Taua Tradition
advances.text: The great war canoes that carry up to a hundred warriors, their carved prows and sternposts announcing the mana of their iwi.

advances.name: Wharenui Tradition
advances.text: The carved meeting houses that serve as centers of tribal governance, ceremony, and the preservation of whakapapa.

advances.name: Gardens of Rongo
advances.text: Gardens are laid out in plots between low rows of stone, and gravel and sand are carried to them to warm the soil, so that the crops of the tropics bear in a colder land. What the gardens, the forest and the sea give is laid up in storehouses raised on posts.

advances.name: Mau Rakau
advances.text: The martial art of wielding traditional weapons (taiaha, tewhatewha, patu) with the balance, timing, and precision that can only come from years of training.

advances.name: Iwi Governance
advances.text: The sophisticated system of chiefly authority, where ariki and rangatira lead through a combination of inherited mana and personal achievement.

advances.name: The Greenstone Trails
advances.text: Trails over the passes of the Southern Alps and canoe routes along the coasts carry greenstone north, and obsidian, argillite and finished adzes pass back along them. Where the trails end, workshops grind stone into tools.

event.title: The Greenstone Trails
event.text:
The greenstone of the South Island, pounamu, has become the most prized material in all of Aotearoa. Found only in the rivers and mountains of Te Wai Pounamu, this nephrite jade is tougher than any other stone of the islands and takes a polish that gleams like the sea. A mere of greenstone or a hei-tiki pendant carries the mana of its owner.

The stone is carried out along the trails of Ngai Tahu, over the passes of the Southern Alps and by canoe along the coasts of both islands. Obsidian, argillite and finished adzes pass back the same way, and gifts of stone bind distant hapu to one another. A single mere pounamu may be worth more than all the food a hapu can grow in a season. The trails are not merely paths; they are an economy.

options.text: Pounamu is the wealth of our nation.

advances.name: Waka Hourua Voyaging
advances.text: The double-hulled ocean canoe capable of crossing vast stretches of open sea, guided by ancestral star navigation and knowledge of ocean currents.

advances.name: Whare Wananga
advances.text: The sacred schools of higher learning where tohunga master whakapapa, astronomy, medicine, and the ritual knowledge that holds Maori society together.

event.title: The Whare Wananga
event.text:
The whare wananga, houses of higher learning, represent the pinnacle of Maori intellectual tradition. Within these sacred institutions, carefully selected students of chiefly lineage spend years memorizing vast bodies of knowledge: whakapapa genealogies stretching back to the arrival of the great canoes, karakia for every occasion, the movements of stars that guide ocean voyages, and the medicinal properties of every plant in the forest.

The tohunga who graduate from these schools are the living repositories of their people's accumulated wisdom. At places like Te Rawheoro in Tolaga Bay, knowledge passes from generation to generation through structured oral instruction that rivals the universities of Europe in its rigor and depth.

options.text: Knowledge is the true taonga of our people.

advances.name: Rahui Conservation
advances.text: The system of temporary resource bans, rahui, that allow depleted fishing grounds, forests, and gardens to recover, ensuring sustainable use of the land.

advances.name: Harakeke Weaving
advances.text:
The art of weaving harakeke flax into cloaks, baskets, ropes, and sails, an industry that produces both everyday necessities and treasured ceremonial garments.

Available in: Adze Makers' Workshop

advances.name: Star Navigation
advances.text: The ancient Polynesian science of wayfinding by the stars, ocean swells, and the flight of birds, a navigational tradition that conquered the Pacific.

advances.name: Hapu Alliances
advances.text: The complex web of inter-tribal relationships, marriage alliances, and gift exchanges that bind hapu together in times of peace and war.

advances.name: European Contact Trade
advances.text:
The arrival of European traders and whalers opens new markets for Maori agricultural produce, flax, and timber. The ships pay for their pigs and potatoes in muskets.

Available in: Adze Makers' Workshop

advances.name: Whalebone Artistry
advances.text:
The transformation of whale bone into finely carved weapons, ornaments, and ritual objects, a tradition that elevates raw material into expressions of tribal identity.

Available in: Adze Makers' Workshop

advances.name: Potato Revolution
advances.text: The rapid adoption of the European potato transforms Maori agriculture. Easier to grow than kumara and producing far greater yields, the potato fuels a population boom and commercial surplus.

advances.name: Tupara Musketeers
advances.text: The adoption of the double-barrelled shotgun, tupara, by Maori warriors, who modify the weapons for faster firing and adapt their tactics accordingly.

advances.name: Tribal Mana
advances.text: The accumulated prestige and spiritual authority of the nation, the mana that comes from military victories, successful harvests, and the achievements of great chiefs.

advances.name: Inter-Island Trade
advances.text: Maori trading networks connecting the North and South Islands, carrying pounamu northward and agricultural surplus southward in waka and later European-style vessels.

advances.name: Pa Adaptation
advances.text: The first modifications to traditional pa design in response to new threats, deeper ditches, stronger palisades, and new approaches to defensive positioning.

advances.name: Musket Adaptation
advances.text: The full integration of firearms into Maori warfare, including modified muskets with enlarged touch holes for faster firing and the tactical use of volley fire from fortified positions.

event.title: The Musket Wars
event.text:
The arrival of European firearms has transformed warfare in Aotearoa utterly. Chiefs who acquire muskets first hold devastating advantage over those who still fight with taiaha and mere. Hongi Hika of Ngapuhi demonstrated this when he returned from England in 1821 with hundreds of muskets, launching raids that reached from the Bay of Islands to the shores of Lake Rotorua.

But the Maori genius for adaptation runs deep. Within a generation, every major iwi has armed itself, and our engineers have redesigned the traditional pa to withstand the new weapons. The gunfighter pa, with its zigzag trenches, double palisades, and underground bunkers, may be the most sophisticated indigenous fortification system in the world.

Will we embrace the offensive power of the musket, or master the defensive art of the new pa?

options.text: Arm every warrior. The musket changes everything.

modifiers.name: Ahi Ka: The Musket's Fire
modifiers.text: The thunder of the musket has changed warfare forever. Chiefs like Hongi Hika have shown that those who master the new weapons first can reshape the balance of power across all of Aotearoa.

options.text: Fortify and endure. The pa will protect us.

modifiers.name: Ahi Ka: The Gunfighter Pa
modifiers.text: Our pa have been rebuilt for a new kind of war. Zigzag trenches, double palisades, and underground bunkers turn every fortification into a death trap for attackers wielding muskets and cannon alike.

advances.name: Gunfighter Pa
advances.text: The revolutionary redesign of the pa for firearms warfare, zigzag trenches, double palisades with flax padding, underground bunkers, and communication tunnels.

advances.name: Commercial Agriculture
advances.text: The rapid expansion of Maori farming to supply European settlements and visiting ships. Within decades, iwi are producing tonnes of potatoes, wheat, and pork for export.

advances.name: Whalers' Economy
advances.text: Maori engagement with the shore whaling industry, providing labor, food, and coastal access in exchange for European goods and technology.

advances.name: Taua Warfare
advances.text: The organized war parties, taua, that combine traditional warrior discipline with musket firepower, striking with devastating speed across great distances. Each is a party of kin raised for one season's campaign.

advances.name: He Whakaputanga Sovereignty
advances.text: The Declaration of Independence of the United Tribes of New Zealand, signed in 1835, asserting Maori sovereignty and establishing a framework for self-governance.

advances.name: Trading Vessels
advances.text:
Maori-owned and operated trading ships that carry agricultural produce between settlements and across the Tasman to Sydney, a maritime commercial fleet rivaling colonial efforts.

Available in: Waka Shipyard

advances.name: Kingitanga
advances.text: The Maori King Movement, a pan-tribal institution uniting iwi under a single sovereign to resist land alienation and assert collective Maori governance.

event.title: The Kingitanga
event.text:
In the face of growing pressure on Maori lands and sovereignty, a movement has emerged to unite the iwi under a single monarch. At Pukawa, on the shores of Lake Taupo, the great chief Potatau Te Wherowhero has been nominated as the first Maori King. The Kingitanga, the King Movement, represents the most ambitious attempt at pan-tribal unity in Maori history.

The movement's supporters argue that only a united Maori nation can resist the loss of lands and the erosion of sovereignty. But the question of how to achieve this unity divides opinion. Some believe armed resistance is the only answer. Others argue that the Kingitanga's greatest power lies in presenting a united diplomatic front, speaking with one voice for all Maori.

options.text: The King shall lead us in war if need be.

modifiers.name: Kotahitanga: Armed Resistance
modifiers.text: Under the Maori King, the iwi have united not merely in council but in arms. The land will be defended by force, and no foreign power will take what is ours without a fight.

options.text: The King shall speak for all Maori with one voice.

modifiers.name: Kotahitanga: United Voice
modifiers.text: The Kingitanga speaks for all Maori with one voice. Through diplomacy and unity of purpose, we will secure our sovereignty and our lands through negotiation rather than bloodshed.

advances.name: Modern Pa Warfare
advances.text: The sophisticated defensive systems of the New Zealand Wars, where pa like Ruapekapeka combine underground bunkers, enfilading trench lines, and tactical depth to defeat professional armies.

advances.name: Maori Commerce
advances.text: The flourishing of Maori commercial enterprise, flour mills, trading vessels, wheat exports, proving that indigenous economy can compete on equal terms with colonial commerce.

advances.name: Kotahitanga
advances.text: The unity movement that brings together Maori leaders in parliaments and councils to address shared concerns through collective action and mutual support.

advances.name: Cultural Renaissance
advances.text: A flowering of Maori arts, language, and identity, the determination to preserve and revitalize the traditions that define what it means to be Maori.

advances.name: Land Resistance
advances.text: The fierce defense of Maori lands against alienation, through legal challenge, passive resistance, and when necessary, armed opposition.

advances.name: Runanga Councils
advances.text: The tribal council system, runanga, that provides structured governance, dispute resolution, and collective decision-making across Maori society.

destiny.name: Destiny of Aotearoa
destiny.text: With the iwi united under a single sovereignty, Aotearoa stands at a crossroads. The path chosen at formation now opens into a grand national destiny. Stability and purpose will guide the way forward.

event.title: The Destiny of Aotearoa
event.text:
The islands are united, the iwi speak as one. Now a greater question presents itself: what shall Aotearoa become? The ancestors who crossed the Pacific in nothing but waka hourua could not have imagined the nation that has risen from their landing places. But they would recognize the ambition, the drive to push beyond every horizon, that burns in the hearts of their descendants.

Our destiny awaits.

options.text: Ka tu tatou, we shall rise!

destiny.name: Te Ara o Tu
destiny.text: Claim dominion over Tamaki Makaurau and project power beyond the horizon to the island of Niue. The mana of the confederation must be known on every shore before the war parties of Tu, the god of war, put to sea.

conditions.text: Own Tāmaki Makaurau, or a subject owns it
Own Niue, or a subject owns it

event.title: Consolidation of the Islands
event.text:
Tamaki Makaurau, the city of a hundred lovers, the isthmus between two harbors, serves as our base of power. And beyond the horizon, the island of Niue has fallen under the mana of our warriors, the first conquest beyond Aotearoa's home waters.

With this foothold in the wider Pacific, our toa look further outward. The ocean stretches before us, studded with island kingdoms that could fall under the sovereignty of a truly ambitious nation.

options.text: The islands are ours. Now we look beyond.

destiny.name: Pacific Taua
destiny.text: The war parties of Aotearoa sail beyond the horizon in the great waka taua. Tongatapu of Tonga and the great islands of Fiji must fall under our mana. The wealth of conquest funds the next campaign.

conditions.text: Own Tongatapu, or a subject owns it
Own Kubuna, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Pacific Taua
event.text:
Our war canoes have crossed open ocean to bring the mana of Aotearoa to distant shores. The kingdoms of Tonga and the chiefdoms of Fiji have been brought under our sovereignty, the first time a Polynesian power has projected force so far beyond its home waters.

The veterans of these campaigns return with new knowledge and confidence. Some argue for honing our offensive capabilities to press even further. Others believe the priority should be consolidating control over these vast new territories, binding the conquered peoples to our cause through integration and shared purpose.

options.text: Sharpen the taiaha for the next campaign.

modifiers.name: Te Patu: The Strike
modifiers.text: The warriors of Aotearoa have perfected the art of the decisive strike, swift, overwhelming, and unstoppable. Our campaigns begin before the enemy even knows we are coming.

options.text: Bind these peoples to our mana.

modifiers.name: Te Mana Motuhake: Sovereign Authority
modifiers.text: The conquered peoples recognize the mana of Aotearoa. Through integration and shared purpose, the new territories are bound to the crown, though the rapid expansion strains the treasury.

destiny.name: Mana Whenua
destiny.text: The great southern land beckons, and the double-hulled voyaging canoes can cross the Tasman. Plant the taiaha among the Eora on the shores of Botany Bay and claim the lands of the Dharug people. Only the mightiest nation, rich in gold and steeped in prestige, can accomplish this.

conditions.text: Own Eora, or a subject owns it
Own Dharug, or a subject owns it

event.title: Mana Whenua: The Great Southern Land
event.text:
The impossible has been achieved. The warriors of Aotearoa have crossed the Tasman and planted their standard on the shores of the great southern continent. The lands around Botany Bay, vast, fertile, and rich in resources, now answer to a Maori sovereign.

This is the apex of Aotearoa's martial destiny, a conquest that dwarfs anything the ancestors could have imagined. But holding such territory demands a choice: do we pursue total military dominance, reinforcing our armies at the expense of all else? Or do we settle these new lands, assimilating the local peoples and building a civilization that can endure?

modifiers.name: Te Pakanga Nui: The Great War
modifiers.text: Total war mobilization sustains the conquest of the southern continent. Every resource is directed to reinforcing armies and maintaining the campaign, at the cost of diplomatic relationships.

options.text: Settle and build; this land is ours now.

modifiers.name: Te Nohoanga: The Settlement
modifiers.text: The settlers follow the warriors, planting kumara and building pa on the shores of a new land. Control is established through occupation and assimilation, though the cost of construction in these distant lands runs high.

destiny.name: Te Ara o Tangaroa
destiny.text: The bounty of Tangaroa flows through our markets. Build a fishing and trading economy worthy of the ocean god, accumulating wealth and maintaining the stability needed for long voyages.

conditions.text: A market the country is in

children.text: Fish is produced in the market
Fish is traded in the market

event.title: The Ocean Road
event.text:
The markets of Aotearoa overflow with the bounty of Tangaroa. Fish from every coast, pounamu from the rivers of Te Wai Pounamu, and the products of a thriving maritime economy fill our trading vessels. The ancestors who navigated by the stars to reach these islands would approve; we have turned the ocean from a barrier into a highway.

Our merchants range further with each passing year, establishing trade connections that bring wealth and knowledge flooding into our harbors.

options.text: The ocean provides; we shall follow its currents.

destiny.name: Te Hokinga Wairua
destiny.text: The spirit of the great voyaging ancestors returns. The canoes sail back to Rarotonga, from whose Avana passage tradition says the fleet set out, and Waitangi in the Bay of Islands grows from a landing place into a harbour town. A nation of traders, scholars, and mariners.

conditions.text: Own Rarotonga Atoll, or a subject owns it
Waitangi is ours and has grown into a town or become the seat of a market

event.title: Te Hokinga Wairua: The Great Voyaging
event.text:
The spirit of the great voyaging ancestors has returned in a new form. Where they crossed the Pacific with stars and courage, we now build trade networks and institutions that span the ocean. The merchants of our ports finance ventures to distant markets. Our canoes have found the way back to Rarotonga, and the harbour at Waitangi is crowded with ships.

Some see this as the foundation for a true trade empire: our merchants should dominate every market in the Pacific, building grand cities that attract the wealth of the world. Others argue for a different kind of wealth: the exchange of knowledge and culture that comes from welcoming the world to our shores.

options.text: Build the greatest trade empire in the Pacific.

modifiers.name: Te Hokohoko Nui: The Great Trade
modifiers.text: Aotearoa's merchants dominate the Pacific trade routes. Our cities grow into grand entrepots that attract traders from across the ocean, their wealth sustaining the prestige of the nation.

options.text: Welcome the world to our wharenui.

modifiers.name: Te Whanaungatanga: The Kinship
modifiers.text: The principle of whanaungatanga, kinship and connection, extends beyond the iwi to embrace the wider world. Visitors and traders are welcomed, knowledge is exchanged, and Aotearoa prospers through openness.

destiny.name: Te Mana o te Moana
destiny.text: Become the undisputed masters of the Pacific. Build docks in two of our ports, accumulate vast wealth, and carry the mana of Aotearoa to Havai'i, the Hawaiki of the ancestors, where the marae of Taputapuatea stands. Aotearoa then stands among the great maritime powers of the world.

conditions.text: A Dock or a building that replaced it stands in at least 2 of our locations
Own Havai'i, or a subject owns it

event.title: Te Mana o te Moana: Lords of the Pacific
event.text:
Aotearoa has achieved what no Polynesian nation has ever accomplished: a maritime and economic transformation that places it among the great powers of the world. Our fleets patrol waters from New Zealand to the equator, and the homeland of the ancestors at Havai'i answers to Aotearoa. Our shipwrights build in the docks of our own ports without abandoning the wisdom of the ancestors.

This is the pinnacle of the maritime destiny. But even now, there are those who debate how best to wield this power. Shall we build an invincible navy to enforce our will across the Pacific? Or shall we become a nation of knowledge and diplomacy, respected and courted by all, feared by none, but underestimated at the world's peril?

options.text: Our warships shall rule these waters.

modifiers.name: Te Tino Rangatiratanga o te Moana
modifiers.text: Absolute sovereignty over the ocean. Aotearoa's warships patrol the Pacific from horizon to horizon, enforcing trade routes and projecting power that demands the world's recognition.

options.text: Knowledge is the truest form of mana.

modifiers.name: Te Matauranga: The Knowledge
modifiers.text: The greatest treasure is knowledge. Aotearoa's scholars, diplomats, and spies weave a web of influence that extends far beyond what any fleet could achieve, securing the nation's interests through wisdom.

units.name: Toa Warriors
units.text: Elite Maori warriors trained in the martial art of mau rakau, wielding the taiaha staff and patu club with devastating skill. Their battle cry, the haka, strikes fear into any foe.

units.name: Toa Levy
units.text: Warriors of the iwi called to service, fighting with traditional weapons and the fierce determination that defines the Maori martial spirit.

units.name: Tupara Musketeers
units.text: Maori warriors armed with tupara, double-barrelled shotguns loaded with musket balls, modified with enlarged touch holes for rapid firing in close combat.

units.name: Taua
units.text: A musket war party of a few hundred kinsmen. It moves by canoe and forest track faster than any marching column, opens with the haka and a volley, and goes home when the season turns.

units.name: Pa Defenders
units.text: Musket-armed warriors specializing in the defense of gunfighter pa, fighting from zigzag trenches and double palisades with deadly accuracy.

units.name: Waka Taua
units.text: Great war canoes carved from single logs, adorned with spiral carvings and feathered sternposts, carrying scores of toa warriors into battle.

units.name: Waka Hourua
units.text: Double-hulled ocean voyaging canoes capable of crossing vast stretches of open Pacific, guided by the ancient science of Polynesian star navigation.

units.name: Maori Trading Schooner
units.text: European-style sailing vessels owned and crewed by Maori, carrying agricultural surplus between settlements and across the Tasman Sea to Sydney.

buildings.name: Pa
buildings.text: A fortified hilltop settlement with multiple defensive terraces, wooden palisades, and fighting stages, the backbone of Maori territorial defense.

buildings.name: Whare Wananga
buildings.text: A sacred school of higher learning where tohunga preserve and transmit the accumulated knowledge of the Maori people across generations.

buildings.name: Wharenui
buildings.text: A carved meeting house adorned with intricate carvings that encode tribal genealogy and history, serving as the center of community governance and ceremony.

buildings.name: Adze Makers' Workshop
buildings.text: A workshop at the end of the stone trails, where blocks of argillite and basalt are flaked and ground into adzes and chisels, the tools that fell the trees and shape the canoes. Weavers and bone carvers work beside the adze makers.

buildings.name: Pataka
buildings.text: A storehouse raised on posts, out of reach of rats and damp, its front carved to show the wealth of the hapu. Preserved birds, dried fish and fern root are kept in it through the winter.

buildings.name: Maori Flour Mill
buildings.text: A water mill on the stream below the wheat fields, grinding the iwi's own harvest into flour for the markets of Auckland and Sydney.

where.text: The location's raw material is Wheat

buildings.name: Waka Shipyard
buildings.text: A shipbuilding yard where Maori craftsmen construct both traditional waka and European-style trading vessels.

buildings.name: Runanga House
buildings.text: A formal council house where tribal leaders gather to deliberate matters of governance, justice, and collective action.

buildings.name: Musket Pa
buildings.text: A fortification rebuilt for the age of firearms, double palisades with flax padding, zigzag trenches for musket fire, and reinforced gates to withstand assault.

buildings.name: Kotahitanga Hall
buildings.text: A pan-tribal assembly hall where Maori leaders from across the motu gather to discuss matters affecting all iwi, the physical embodiment of unity.

buildings.name: Te Whare Toa
buildings.text: A great warrior training hall where the martial traditions of Aotearoa, from the ancient art of mau rakau to modern combined arms warfare, are passed from generation to generation.

buildings.name: Te Whare Taonga
buildings.text: A great treasure house and trading emporium on the coast, where the wealth of the Pacific flows through Maori hands, pounamu, silk, spices, and the products of a dozen island nations.

list.name: Rangatiratanga
list.text: The rangatira (chief) and ariki (paramount chief) lead the iwi and hapu by inherited mana and personal authority, advised at every step by the koroua elder council. Authority is consensual, not coercive: a rangatira who loses mana loses followers, and the confederation of tribes is held together by mutual recognition between these chiefly councils rather than by any single sovereign decree. Maintained well, the system gives the realm a deep reservoir of legitimate local governors; neglected, it dissolves back into the autonomy of the constituent iwi.

list.name: Tohunga me te Whare Wananga
list.text: The tohunga were specialists who held the most tapu knowledge of the iwi: the whakapapa genealogies, the star-paths and sea-roads, the carving of pounamu and the working of timber, the healing arts, and the karakia ritual that opened or closed every undertaking. Their apprentices learned in the whare wananga, sacred learning houses where knowledge was transmitted orally across generations. To dismantle the tohunga class was to sever the lineage of memory itself, but a corrupt or self-serving priesthood could turn that same authority into a private monopoly on truth.

list.name: Whakapakari Pa
list.text: The pa was a hilltop or peninsula settlement defended by ditches, palisades, fighting platforms, and (after European contact) musket-loopholed terraces. Every iwi maintained multiple pa keyed to seasonal campaigns and as refuges in war, built and repaired by communal labour drawn from the surrounding hapu. The network gave Aotearoa a defensive depth that would baffle British generals in the New Zealand Wars of the 1860s, but the labour obligation fell on the cultivators, who paid in kumara and sweat for walls they did not always wish to build.

list.name: Muru me Utu
list.text: The customary law of restitution and reciprocity. Muru was the ritualised plundering raid by which an offended hapu took property from the offender's kin to restore the balance broken by a breach of tapu or an insult to mana. Utu was the broader principle that demanded every gift, injury, and honour be answered in kind. Together they constituted a community-enforced legal order that bypassed any chief's command: mana was preserved, the people fed, and feuds endured across generations while the central state's writ remained correspondingly thin.

list.name: Te Kingitanga
list.text: In 1858 the chiefs of the central North Island gathered at Ngaruawahia and elected Te Wherowhero Potatau the first Maori king. Modelled in part on the British monarchy that the chiefs had observed since the Treaty of Waitangi of 1840, the Kingitanga aimed to halt the alienation of ancestral land by uniting the iwi under a single sovereign capable of negotiating with the Crown on equal terms. As an institution it represents the moment when iwi-confederation hardens into national kingship: the price paid in rangatira independence, the gain in unified legitimacy.
